## The State Is the Complete Snapshot {#sec-lay-ch03}

## A Concrete Picture

Two photographs can look identical and conceal opposite futures. In the first,
a playground swing has reached its highest point and is about to fall. In the
second, it is moving upward through the same angle and is about to slow. The
seat, chains, and child occupy nearly the same places in both photographs. Yet
one moment leads downward and the other upward because velocity is missing from
the picture.

Now photograph a flexible beam only at its two ends. Different bends inside the
span can leave those endpoints in the same places while storing different elastic
energy. The photograph has missed deformation. Changing the material or rest
shape is a different comparison: it changes the model parameters. For a fixed
elastic law, complete deformation determines strain energy; energy is not an
independently adjustable hidden quantity. Two muscles at the same joint angle can
likewise have different activation or internal tissue states and respond
differently to a disturbance.

A useful dynamics model gathers everything it needs to continue the motion into
a **state**. For a rigid double pendulum, the state may consist of two angles and
two angular velocities. For a flexible club, it also includes shaft deflection
and deflection rate. For an actuator with first-order lag, it may include an
activation state. A pure time delay instead requires relevant past history, or a
declared finite-dimensional approximation. A compliant contact may require
interface deformation, friction memory, and a contact mode. The complete snapshot
is more than a pose.

![State Components and the Additional Conditions Required for Prediction.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_state_snapshot.svg){#fig-lay-state-snapshot width=94% fig-alt="Configuration, velocity, and internal variables feed a present-state box. Prediction additionally requires the model and parameters, future inputs, initial time, and well-posed evolution rules; state alone does not specify future commands."}

## How the Mechanism Works

The formal state is commonly written $\mathbf x$. For a two-link planar model,
one convenient choice is

$$
\mathbf x = [q_1, q_2, \dot q_1, \dot q_2]^\mathsf T,
$$

where $q_1$ and $q_2$ describe configuration and the dotted variables describe
angular velocity. The equations of motion define a rule

$$
\dot{\mathbf x}=f(\mathbf x,\mathbf u,t),
$$

which says: given the present state, the present control $\mathbf u$, and any
explicit time dependence, compute the rate at which the state changes. A
numerical integrator advances that rule through many small steps.

The word *state* has a strict purpose. Within a declared model, it contains the
information about the past needed to evolve from the present. Identical states
produce identical futures **when the same model, parameters, initial time,
future inputs, and well-posed evolution rules are used**. State alone does not
supply tomorrow's commands. In a nonautonomous model, starting the same state at
a different clock time can also change the future.

Well-posedness matters. A single-valued deterministic right-hand side does not
by itself guarantee uniqueness: $\dot x=\sqrt{x}$ for $x\geq0$, starting at zero,
admits both a permanently zero solution and a solution that waits before growing.
A common sufficient uniqueness condition is local Lipschitz continuity in state,
with appropriate regularity of the inputs; it is not a necessary condition in
every model. The claim concerns times for which the solution exists in the
model's valid domain, not an unconditional forecast forever.

Contacts and impacts may require more than the displayed smooth ODE. Specify
constraint consistency, discrete modes, event guards, and reset rules, and verify
that they define a unique admissible evolution for the comparison. An impact can
reset velocity while leaving configuration continuous. Numerical time stepping
and tolerances approximate this declared evolution; disagreement between
simulations can reveal numerical error or ill-posedness as well as missing state.

### Configuration Is More Than a Photograph

Configuration describes where the modeled bodies are within their allowed
geometry. In a planar double pendulum, two angles may be enough. In a spatial
golfer model, configuration can include pelvis position and orientation, spinal
and shoulder rotations, elbow and wrist coordinates, club pose, and perhaps
shaft modes. Rotations require care because three-dimensional orientation is not
just three independent slider positions. Different angle sequences can describe
the same physical orientation, and some parameterizations contain singularities.
With redundant orientation coordinates, coordinate rates and physical angular
velocity are different objects: a kinematic map can relate $\dot q$ to a velocity
vector $v$. Normalization and closed-chain constraints restrict admissible states;
arbitrary coordinate and velocity arrays need not describe a possible motion.

Configuration also determines mechanical advantage. The mass matrix, moment
arms, constraint Jacobian, generalized gravity forces, and mapping from joint
torques to club acceleration can change with posture. Gravity need not change
direction in an inertial frame; its body-frame components and generalized
projections depend on configuration. The same torque vector applied at
two configurations can produce different accelerations. State-dependent
geometry is therefore not scenery around the mechanism; it is part of the
mechanism.

### Velocity Gives the Snapshot a Direction

Velocity tells how configuration is changing. For ordinary rigid-body mechanics
in independent coordinates, write the mechanical part as

$$
\begin{aligned}
M(q)\ddot q&=\tau-c(q,\dot q)\\
&\quad-g(q)-D\dot q,
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $q$ and $\tau$ are coordinate and generalized-torque vectors. With positive
inertias and a regular independent-coordinate description, $M$ is positive
definite and can be inverted to obtain acceleration. The vector $c$ collects
quadratic Coriolis and centrifugal terms, $g$ is the
potential-force term, and $D\dot q$ illustrates viscous resistance. At the same
configuration, $M(q)$ is the **same matrix**. Reversing every velocity reverses
momentum $M\dot q$ and, for a fixed torque, power $\tau^{\mathsf T}\dot q$, but leaves
quadratic
$c(q,\dot q)$ unchanged: each product contains two velocity factors. The matrix
factorization $C(q,\dot q)$ can change sign while its product
$c=C(q,\dot q)\dot q$ stays the same. Viscous resistance changes sign instead.
These statements apply to this model class; rotating-frame, magnetic, or other
odd-in-velocity forces need separate treatment.

Consequently, in the undamped model, opposite velocities can yield **equal
instantaneous accelerations** under the same posture and torque. Their futures
still differ because their initial velocities differ. Acceleration is only the
velocity derivative, not the full state derivative. Reversing just one joint's
velocity, or changing speed magnitudes, can change quadratic coupling terms.
Large velocity-dependent effects therefore do not imply that every reversal
changes every term.

Velocity is also needed to evaluate power. A $100$-newton force at a stationary
point delivers zero instantaneous translational power. The same force at a point
moving $5$ metres per second in its direction delivers $500$ watts. Reverse the
velocity and the power is $-500$ watts. Force without velocity cannot tell the
energy story.

### Stored Variables Carry History Into the Present

Rigid-body coordinates and velocities are not always enough. A flexible shaft
has modal displacement and velocity. A series-elastic actuator may have tendon
stretch. A first-order activation model has a state that lags its neural command.
A transmission model with an evolving deflection can use that state to determine
engagement. A memoryless dead-zone map alone does not acquire an independent
state merely because it is nonlinear. These variables are **history summarized**:
they contain the past information needed to continue under specified future
inputs. Once two histories lead to the same sufficient state, their earlier
histories need not remain separate predictors in that model.

This matters directly to preload. In the finite-preparation experiment, both
programs begin relaxed, build their own transmission deflections for $180$ ms,
and carry those states continuously through transition. Continuity holds
**within each branch**; the two strategies need not have the same internal state
at transition. Comparing their futures tests the effect of preparation and its
resulting state under the declared later commands, not the isolated effect of a
new command from identical states. Chapter 14 of this companion gives the model
and its limits.
Finite preparation also need not reach equilibrium to avoid a state reset.

Pure delay is a different kind of memory. For a scalar channel $y(t)=u(t-d)$, two past input
histories can have the same current value $u(0)$ and identical future commands,
but yield different outputs during the next $d$ seconds. One must retain the
relevant history over $[-d,0]$, not only the current command. Replacing that
history with a first-order lag is a modeling approximation with different
transient behavior; assess it over the frequencies and time scales used in the
claim.

### State and Input Must Not Be Confused

An input is something the model treats as externally prescribed for the future:
a joint torque command, a desired actuator level, or a measured base trajectory.
A state is something the model evolves. The distinction can change between
model tiers. A prescribed hand path can be a kinematic input to an
inverse-dynamics model; it does not determine every joint motion or internal force
without additional measurements and constraints. In a forward model driven by
joint torques, the hand path can instead be an outcome. A prescribed pelvis
motion can hide the reaction of the club on the body; a dynamically coupled
moving-base model can let that feedback alter the state. A base trajectory
prescribed in advance still prevents that response.

If a controller generates commands from measurements, its memory also belongs in
the closed-loop state, or its complete future input must be prescribed. Calling
a signal an input does not mean it is independent of state in the physical
experiment.

This difference explains why two models can answer different questions even if
they draw the same stick figure. An inverse model asks what forces are compatible
with measured motion. A forward model asks what motion results from forces and
an initial state. Neither is automatically superior. They have different
estimands and different opportunities for circular reasoning.

### A Matched-State Intervention

Suppose we want to ask what the current shoulder torque contributes to club
acceleration. One useful experiment freezes the state at an instant and solves
the acceleration twice: once with the recorded torque and once with that torque
set to zero. Hold the entire relevant state, time, parameters, constraints, and
other inputs fixed. Matching configuration and velocity is sufficient for the
simplest rigid model, but not for models with additional actuator or contact
states. The acceleration difference is then a pointwise intervention contrast.
If acceleration is affine in the selected torque at that state and contact mode,
the contrast equals its linear control contribution. For nonlinear control maps,
the contrast remains defined but need not form an additive partition across
actuators.

If we then integrate the zero-torque branch forward, its state begins to diverge.
After a few milliseconds, force and power differences include both the missing
torque and the changed trajectory it caused. That forward counterfactual answers
a persistence question rather than a pure instantaneous attribution question.
Both are legitimate if their contracts are stated. An instantaneous torque step
changes acceleration without itself causing a velocity jump; an impulse or a
contact reset is a different intervention. Zeroing a neural or actuator command
also need not instantly remove transmitted torque when activation or transmission
states persist.

The initial state difference is zero by construction. Fix other inputs,
parameters, disturbances, and either the future open-loop program or the feedback
policy being compared. Numerical divergence beyond tolerance then represents
the declared intervention and its later interactions within that model.
Reoptimizing each future or resetting an internal state changes the question
and requires a new contract.

### Phase Landmarks Need an Event Contract

Golf language uses transition, early downswing, delivery, and impact. A clock
time alone may not align these phases across participants or simulations. An
event can use a position or velocity crossing, a peak criterion, a contact guard,
or a measurement history. Specify the quantity, direction, admissible time
window, which crossing counts, and whether the event must be detected causally.
A velocity peak requires a sign change or comparison over a neighborhood;
retrospective peak labeling differs from real-time detection. Freezing a
criterion in advance limits outcome-driven selection but does not guarantee
that it exists, is unique, or is robust to noise.

Comparing two runs at their respective impact events also differs from comparing
them at a common elapsed time: the intervention may shift the event itself.
Report that timing difference and handle missing events explicitly. Otherwise,
aligning curves can hide part of the effect one intended to measure.

### State-Based Timing Versus Clock-Based Timing

A command labeled 120 milliseconds before impact is not necessarily equivalent
across golfers or clubs. If impact time is known only after the swing, this is
retrospective labeling; a real-time controller needs an estimator or a causally
detectable trigger. One system may already have a small arm--club angle and high
relative speed; another may still be carried with substantial lag. A state-based
rule might refer to relative angle, angular velocity, shaft mode, or the sign of
an interaction term. It may adapt across tempo changes if that variable remains
observable and its threshold predicts the desired response. This advantage needs
testing: a noisy or poorly estimated state trigger can be less reliable than a
clock rule.

The backswing-preload proposal belongs here. Its plausible benefit is not that
one direction of effort is inherently superior. It is that continuous loading
might deliver a transition state with less force-development delay than a full
role reversal. To test that claim, the state must include the modeled
transmission or activation variable. Without those variables, it cannot attribute
an effect to that particular transmission-memory pathway. Other modeled pathways,
such as changed velocity or geometry, could still produce an allocation
difference and must be separated.

### What an Incomplete Observation Can Miss

Now give the club a flexible shaft. The grip and clubhead may occupy the same
visible positions in two trials while unresolved shaft modes or modal rates
differ. For example, a scalar observation $y=a+b$ cannot distinguish modal
amplitudes $(a,b)=(0,0)$ from $(1,-1)$. With unit modal stiffnesses, their elastic
energies $\tfrac12(a^2+b^2)$ differ despite equal $y$. This is an abstract
observability example, not a calibrated shaft. Complete deformation and modal
rates, together with the constitutive law and loading, determine storage and
exchange; visible endpoints alone do not. Add muscle activation and short-range
stiffness, and two outwardly similar states can also resist perturbation differently. “Same position” is
therefore far weaker than “same state.”

### What Must Be Measured

Motion capture provides observations from which model coordinates and velocities
are estimated. Filtering and differentiation affect noise, phase, and uncertainty
near transition. Strain gauges observe strain at selected locations; recovering
shaft modes requires a model and enough independent measurements. Bilateral grip
sensors measure the wrench components they are designed and calibrated to resolve.
EMG records electrical activity; inferred activation timing and force require
additional dynamics and assumptions.

Neither a plausible fit nor a larger sensor count guarantees observability. For
a linear model, observability depends on the state-to-output map and dynamics;
for a nonlinear model it can also depend on trajectory, excitation, operating
point, and parameters. Different states can produce indistinguishable outputs
within measurement precision. A single measured output at one instant is also
different from a time series under known excitation.

Represent uncertainty in states, parameters, sensor calibration, and model choice
as far as the evidence allows. A distribution is conditional on the estimator and
its assumptions, not automatically a calibrated statement of truth. Repeating
counterfactuals across plausible reconstructions tests sensitivity to those
assumptions; it cannot establish a causal human effect or cure a structurally
unidentifiable state by itself.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The “complete snapshot” phrase can suggest that a finite model state contains
all physical reality. It does not. A model state is complete only relative to
the equations chosen. A two-link rigid model omits shaft vibrations, soft tissue,
muscle activation, grip deformation, aerodynamics, and neural feedback. Its
four-number state, specified future inputs, and well-posed rules can determine a
unique future of that reduced model while
remaining a sparse description of a human swing.

Biological systems may also contain memory that simple first-order states do not
capture: muscle history dependence, reflex delays, thixotropy, fatigue, and
learning. Adding every possible state would make estimation impossible. The
scientific task is to add a state when it changes the question or survives a
falsification test, not because complexity sounds realistic.

Finally, measurements never reveal state without uncertainty. Velocities are
often derived from noisy positions. Internal force and activation states may be
only indirectly observed. A responsible model carries those uncertainties into
its conclusions instead of treating one reconstructed trajectory as exact.

**Model Result:** In the registered rigid double-pendulum counterfactual study,
each commanded/killswitch pair begins with the same four-component angle/velocity
state, at the same cut time. The commanded branch continues its declared program;
the other sets both generalized torques to zero. The finite-preparation study
instead preserves each transmission branch's state through its command switch
and deliberately allows preparation to create different states. These are
different experimental contracts, with different causal questions.

**Measurement Boundary:** Motion capture estimates visible kinematics, not a
complete biological state. Inferring velocities, activation, deformation modes,
or contact memory requires a measurement model and uncertainty assumptions.
McPhee's review surveys prescribed-motion, torque-driven, predictive, and contact
models in golf [@mcphee2022]; that survey does not certify a particular sensor set
as a complete state reconstruction.

**Hypothesis:** A golfer may use backswing loading and early-downswing motion to
arrive at a state from which interaction dynamics assist late club acceleration.
That is a state-arrangement hypothesis, not merely a claim about waiting a fixed
number of milliseconds.

**Practical Interpretation:** A pose is the cover of the book, not the page you
are on. To understand what comes next, ask how everything is moving and what
internal elements are already loaded.
